Westmoreland Resources' Payroll, Royalties and Linked Expenditures —
The purpose of this section is to discuss the direct socio-economic consequences of activity generated by Westmoreland Resources' anticipated payroll and direct purchases from local businesses in the impact area. It is also necessary to consider the increased flow of royalty payments that will go to the Crow Tribe as a result of the mining activity.
Table III-3 shows the amounts of wage and salary payments Westmoreland expects to generate under the three development scenarios being considered. The payroll is largest during construction years and decreases in later years with only production employment. The lowest amount of wages and salaries in any one year is a little under $3 million. Under their most probable production schedule (Scenario 1) the highest payroll is $7,386,500 in 1986, which is the last year of construction. Operations payrolls remain over $7 million from then on until exhaustion of the coal. If high level development (Scenario 2) occurs, the payroll will be in excess of $10 million annually for the last decade of the century. With the high employment requirements associated with conversion (Scenario 3) production employment payroll reaches its peak in 1982 when construction employment payroll is over $50 million, resulting in a total payroll of nearly $56 million. Workers take home almost $20 million in 1986, and payroll levels would remain at that level until 2000.
